links.outcome: Hallucination proportion and response score with vs without retrieval grounding in ophthalmology textbooks
links.effect: Adding book retrieval improved score (mean 13.08 vs 15.14; P=.001) and reduced hallucinations (71/120, 59.2% vs 57/120, 47.4%, P=.02) versus fine-tuned model alone.
links.quote: Incorporating information retrieval from reliable sources, particularly ophthalmology textbooks, further improved the model's response compared with solely the best fine-tuned model (mean 13.08, SD 5.43 vs mean 15.14, SD 4.64; P=.001) and reduced hallucinations (71/120, 59.2% vs 57/120, 47.4%, P=.02).

links.outcome: Ophthalmologist answers ranked best with vs without EyeGPT assistance
links.effect: EyeGPT-assisted ophthalmologists ranked best in accuracy for 94 (78.3%) and trustworthiness for 93 (77.5%) of 120 questions; unassisted ophthalmologists ranked best for 14 (11.7%) and 15 (12.5%).
links.quote: With the assistance of EyeGPT, the answers provided by the ophthalmologists excelled, ranking highest in accuracy and trustworthiness in 94 (78.3%) and 93 (77.5%) of the 120 questions, respectively.

links.outcome: EyeGPT answers compared with unassisted ophthalmologists across four dimensions
links.effect: EyeGPT ranked best more often for understandability (19.2% vs 10%) and empathy (34.2% vs 6.7%) but slightly lower for accuracy (10% vs 11.7%) and trustworthiness (10% vs 12.5%).
links.quote: however, the accuracy and trustworthiness of EyeGPT answers were slightly lower than those by the ophthalmologists (accuracy: 12/120, 10% vs 14/120, 11.7%; trustworthiness: 12/120, 10% vs 15/120, 12.5%), highlighting areas for improvement.

links.outcome: Factual errors and incomplete information in best EyeGPT model answers; performance on rare diseases
links.effect: Rater 1 found factual errors in 35/120 (29.2%) and incomplete information in 23/120 (19.2%); scores lower for rare than common diseases (e.g., best fine-tune 10.33 vs 15.79).
links.quote: Rater 1 identified 5 (5/120, 4.2%) QA pairs as containing unrelated information, 35 (35/120, 29.2%) as containing apparent factual errors, 23 (23/120, 19.2%) as having incomplete information, and 6 (6/120, 5%) exhibiting faulty logic.

links.outcome: Score differences by questioner role (patient vs medical student) across model variants
links.effect: Patient-framed responses scored higher; significant for best fine-tune (13.45 vs 10.99, P=.03) and role-play+database (P=.03) but not for RAG+fine-tune variants (P=.06-.08).
links.quote: This difference reached statistically significant in the best fine-tune and role-play+database models.
